content: Citral, also known as 3,7-dimethyl-2,6-octadienal or lemonal, is a compound that exists as two terpenoid isomers with the molecular formula C10H16O. These isomers are distinguished by the configuration of their double bonds. The trans isomer is referred to as geranial or citral A, while the cis isomer is known as neral or citral B. Geranial is characterized by a strong lemon-like odor, whereas neral has a lemon scent that is less intense but sweeter in nature. Citral is widely used as an aromatic compound in perfumery due to its distinct citrus fragrance. It is also employed as a flavoring agent and is used to enhance or fortify lemon oil. Additionally, citral exhibits potent antimicrobial properties and has pheromonal effects in certain insect species. It plays a significant role in the chemical synthesis of compounds such as vitamin A, ionone, and methylionone. This compound is naturally found in the essential oils of various plants. For example, it constitutes 90-95% of the oil from lemon myrtle, 70-85% of the oil from Litsea cubeba, 65-85% of the oil from lemongrass, and 30-35% of the oil from lemon verbena. It is also present in smaller amounts in lemon balm, as well as in the oils of lemons and oranges. From a health and safety perspective, individuals with perfume allergies should avoid exposure to citral, as it may trigger allergic reactions.
